intro: The Hanuman Aarti is a short devotional hymn sung in praise of Hanuman, offered typically at the close of worship when the lamp (deepak) is waved before the deity's image. Like most aartis in household and temple use across North India, its author is not firmly recorded, and tradition simply calls it a Tulsidas composition, a point touched at its end though not something that can be verified as fact. The Hanuman Aarti gathers, in a handful of verses, the central episodes of Hanuman's service to Ram - his strength, his leap to Lanka, his rescue of Lakshman, and his unwavering devotion. It is written to be sung aloud, with clapping and a bell, rather than read silently, and that performative character shapes everything about how the text is structured and used.

groups.heading: The opening call to arati
groups.body: The aarti opens with a direct invitation to perform the aarti for 'Hanuman lala', an affectionate term for Hanuman as a beloved child-figure of Ram's household. This refrain, which recurs through the hymn, names him as the one whose power acts as an instrument of Raghunath, that is, of Ram. It sets the devotional frame for everything that follows: this is not a narrative recited for information, but a hymn sung while the act of worship - the waving of the lit lamp - is actually taking place.

groups.heading: His strength and protective nature
groups.body: The next lines describe Hanuman's strength as so immense that mountains are said to tremble before it, and add that sickness and affliction do not come near one who stays close to him. This is presented as the tradition's own language about Hanuman's character - a protector whose nearness is thought to keep trouble at a distance - rather than a claim being made by the website. He is called the son of Anjani, a great giver of strength, and a constant help to his devotees (santan ke prabhu), establishing him early in the aarti as a helper figure rooted in both power and compassion.

groups.heading: Being sent across the ocean to Lanka
groups.body: This section recalls the moment Hanuman is dispatched by Ram to cross into Lanka, set fire to parts of the city, and bring back news of Sita. The verses mention Lanka's fortifications and the sea surrounding it as obstacles, noting that Hanuman, son of the wind (Pavanputra), crossed without delay. The aarti treats this episode briefly, as a hymn does, trusting that listeners already know the fuller story from the Ramayana rather than narrating it in detail.

groups.heading: Burning Lanka and aiding Ram's mission
groups.body: Here the hymn speaks of Hanuman setting Lanka ablaze, overcoming the asuras (demons) there, and generally furthering Ram and Sita's cause. It is a compressed summary of his wartime role, framed entirely in terms of service - his actions are described as being in support of 'Siyaram ji's' purpose, not as independent heroics. This keeps the devotional focus of the aarti fixed on Hanuman's relationship to Ram rather than on battle imagery for its own sake.

groups.heading: Lakshman's rescue and the Sanjeevani episode
groups.body: This group of verses refers to the well-known episode where Lakshman falls unconscious on the battlefield at dawn, and Hanuman brings the Sanjeevani herb to revive him, saving his life. It is one of the most recognisable moments associated with Hanuman in popular memory, and its inclusion in the aarti signals how central this act of rescue is to how he is remembered and invoked by devotees seeking his help in difficulty.

groups.heading: The descent into Patal and Ahiravana
groups.body: The text then turns to a lesser-known episode, Hanuman entering the netherworld (Patal), overcoming the forces of Yama there, and defeating the asura Ahiravana by tearing off his arms. It further describes one arm striking down demon forces and the other extending protection to devotees. This is a more esoteric part of the aarti, drawn from later Ramayana-related tellings rather than Valmiki's text, and reflects how popular devotional literature absorbed additional stories over time.

groups.heading: Gods and sages performing the aarti
groups.body: This section pictures gods, humans, and sages together performing aarti to Hanuman, chanting 'jai jai jai Hanuman', with a golden plate and camphor flame, and specifically mentions Anjana, his mother, conducting the worship. It shifts the hymn's perspective - rather than recounting Hanuman's deeds, it now depicts a scene of collective devotion, placing the listener's own act of singing the aarti within that same imagined gathering of worshippers.

groups.heading: The closing verse and attribution to Tulsidas
groups.body: The final verses state that one who sings this aarti dwells in Vaikuntha and attains the highest state, language the text itself uses and which tradition repeats rather than something claimed independently here. It closes by crediting Ram with Lanka's destruction and naming Tulsidas as the one who sang this praise, a signature line common to many aartis attributed to him, before the hymn returns to its opening refrain.

recitation: The Hanuman Aarti is most commonly sung in the evening, at the end of a longer worship session, right as the lamp is lit and waved before Hanuman's image - this is what 'aarti' as a ritual act refers to. Many households and temples include it as part of daily worship, while it becomes especially prominent on Tuesdays and Saturdays, days traditionally associated with Hanuman, and during Hanuman Jayanti. People often sing the Hanuman Aarti standing, with hands folded or holding a small bell, and it is frequently sung along with or right after the Hanuman Chalisa, forming a familiar pairing in temple routines. There is no fixed count prescribed for the Hanuman Aarti the way there sometimes is for a chalisa's repetitions - it is generally sung once at the close of worship, by the person performing the puja while others present join in the refrain. In many communities it is also sung communally, with a group gathered around the lamp, clapping to the rhythm. These are customs observed across North Indian devotional practice rather than a single fixed rule.
tradition: Within devotional tradition, the Hanuman Aarti is understood as an act of closing worship - a way of formally honouring Hanuman once the main prayer or reading is complete, by offering him light, sound, and voice together. The text's own closing lines state that one who sings it attains a high spiritual state, language that belongs to the hymn itself and is repeated by devotees as part of its devotional meaning rather than as a claim made independently here. Hanuman is widely regarded in this tradition as a figure of protection, strength, and steady devotion to Ram, and the Hanuman Aarti is one of the shorter, more accessible ways that devotees express reverence toward him on a daily or weekly basis. It is held, in the tradition, to be less a historical record and more a devotional summary - a way of keeping the memory of his service to Ram present in ordinary acts of worship, sung by families, by temple groups, and by individuals alike.

faq.a: The author is recorded as unknown in the strict sense, though popular tradition attributes it to Tulsidas, largely because the final verse names him. There is no independent historical confirmation of this authorship, so it is best understood as a traditional attribution rather than an established fact.

faq.q: When should the Hanuman Aarti be sung?
faq.a: It is traditionally sung at the close of worship, in the evening, when the lamp is waved before Hanuman's image. It is especially common on Tuesdays and Saturdays and during Hanuman Jayanti, though many households include it as part of regular daily puja throughout the week.

faq.q: Is the Hanuman Aarti the same as the Hanuman Chalisa?
faq.a: No, they are different texts. The Hanuman Chalisa is a longer forty-verse composition detailing Hanuman's qualities and deeds, while the aarti is a short hymn specifically meant to accompany the lamp-waving ritual. They are often sung one after the other in the same worship session.

faq.q: Do I need to sing the Hanuman Aarti a fixed number of times?
faq.a: There is no widely fixed count attached to the aarti the way some mantras are repeated a set number of times. It is typically sung once, at the point in worship when the aarti lamp is being offered, with everyone present joining in the refrain.

faq.q: What does the ending of the Hanuman Aarti mean?
faq.a: The closing lines state that one who sings this aarti attains a high spiritual state and credit Ram with Lanka's destruction, before naming Tulsidas. This is the hymn's own traditional language of praise, understood by devotees as part of its devotional close rather than a separate promise made on its behalf.
